passages.t: The Galileans, and the tower that fell
passages.happening:
Some people tell Jesus about “the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices” (verse 1).

Jesus answers, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this fate? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish” (verses 2-3).

Then he names another disaster himself. Eighteen people were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them. “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish” (verses 4-5).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this.

The first event was an act of violence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea. Some Galileans had come to offer sacrifices, most likely at the temple in Jerusalem, and Pilate's soldiers had killed them there, so that their blood mixed with the blood of the animals they brought. No other ancient writer tells of this event. But it fits what is known of Pilate. The Jewish writer Philo, who lived at the time, charged him with violence and cruelty, and the historian Josephus tells how he provoked the people of Jerusalem. Both accounts are hostile to him, but they agree that he was a harsh ruler.

The second was an accident. Siloam was the area at the south end of Jerusalem around the Pool of Siloam, whose remains were found in 2004. A tower there, perhaps part of the city wall, fell and killed eighteen people. No other ancient record tells of it, and where exactly the tower stood is not known.

So Jesus speaks of two kinds of death that still fill the news: one caused by cruel men, one by a building that gave way. And many people then, as now, wondered whether those who died had somehow deserved it. The news may have been brought to Jesus with exactly that question in mind.
passages.ot:
The idea that suffering proves guilt is old. Job's friends held it. One of them asked, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). At the end of the book God says to them, “you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (Job 42:7).

And God does not want anyone to perish: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).
passages.hard:
Were the people who died worse sinners? Jesus says no, twice: ‘No, I tell you.’ Suffering is not a measure of guilt. The people Pilate killed and the people under the tower were no worse than anyone else. Jesus says the same about the man born blind: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). Anyone who tells a grieving family that a death was a punishment is saying what Jesus refused to say.

Then what does ‘unless you repent, you too will all perish’ mean? It is a call to everyone listening, the people who brought the news included. It is not a threat to the bereaved, and it is not an explanation of why anyone died. Jesus turns the question around. Instead of asking ‘What did they do?’, ask ‘Where do I stand with God?’ Every life is short and uncertain, and no one is safer than the people in the news. To repent means to turn back to God. Many readers also hear a warning about Jerusalem itself, where many died when the Romans destroyed the city in AD 70 (19:43-44). Others hear a warning about the final judgment. Both readings hear the same call: turn to God now.

If you have lost someone to violence, or to an accident or disaster, this passage does not say they deserved it. Jesus says the opposite. Grief is not unbelief. If grief is crushing you, do not carry it alone. Reach out to people you trust, to a pastor, or to someone trained to help.
passages.asks: When disaster strikes others, it is tempting to look for a reason that keeps us safe: they must have done something. Jesus will not let us do that. Ask whether you have ever thought, even quietly, that someone's suffering was what they deserved. And ask the question he turns back to you: if your life ended today, where would you stand with God?

passages.t: One more year for the fig tree
passages.happening:
Jesus tells a parable. A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. For three years he has come looking for fruit on it and found none. “Therefore cut it down!” he tells the keeper of the vineyard. “Why should it use up the soil?” (verse 7).

The keeper answers, ‘Sir, leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down’ (verses 8-9). The story ends there.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this parable. Mark and Matthew tell of Jesus cursing a fig tree that had no fruit (Mark 11:12-14; Matthew 21:18-19). Luke has no cursing. He has this story instead, of a tree given one more year.

This fig tree grew in a vineyard, among the vines. Three years was long enough to know the tree was not bearing. A tree that bears nothing still takes water and goodness from the ground that other plants could use. So the owner's request is reasonable.

The keeper does not argue that the tree is good. He asks for time, and he offers to work: dig around it, loosen the soil, put manure on its roots. He will do everything he can to help it bear.

The story is told right after ‘unless you repent’. Its point is that there is still time, and that the time is not endless.
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured Israel as God's vineyard. Isaiah sings for God, “What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it? Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit?” (Isaiah 5:4). Micah grieves like a man who finds “no early fig that I crave” (Micah 7:1).

And Scripture speaks of God's patience: the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
passages.hard:
Who is who in the story? Jesus does not say, and readers take it in more than one way. Many hear the owner as God, looking for the fruit of a changed life, and the keeper as Jesus, who asks for mercy and works to help the tree bear. Others are careful not to set God the Father against the Son, as if one wanted judgment and the other mercy; they read the keeper's patience as God's own. Either way, the parable shows mercy that gives time, and real work to help the tree grow.

Why does it end without telling us what happened? Because the hearers are the tree. Whether it bears fruit is the question left to them.
passages.asks: The tree was given one more year, and someone dug around its roots. Ask what fruit God has been looking for in you, and what he might be doing in your life right now to help it grow. The parable ends open. How it ends for you is still being written.

passages.t: A daughter of Abraham set free
passages.happening:
Jesus is teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath. A woman is there who “had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight” (verse 11).

Jesus sees her and calls her over. “Woman, you are set free from your disability” (verse 12). He puts his hands on her, and at once she stands up straight and begins to praise God.

The synagogue leader is indignant. “There are six days for work,” he tells the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath” (verse 14).

“You hypocrites!” the Lord replies. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water? Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?” (verses 15-16). His opponents are ashamed, and the whole crowd rejoices at the wonderful things he is doing.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story.

Eighteen years is a long time to look at the ground. She could not lift her head to see a face. Yet she was in the synagogue on the Sabbath. Notice that she does not ask for anything. Jesus sees her, calls her, speaks to her, and touches her.

The Sabbath, the seventh day, was a gift and a sign of Israel's covenant with God. No work was to be done on it. The synagogue leader's own words show what he thought: healing was work, and it could wait a day. He is not a monster. He is defending the Sabbath as he understood it, and he does it by scolding the crowd, not Jesus.

Jesus answers with the farm. Everyone in the room untied their animals on the Sabbath and took them to drink. Not to do so would be cruel. Jesus uses the same Greek verb, to loose or untie, for the ox and for the woman. If you loose an ox for a few hours' thirst, should not a woman be loosed after eighteen years?

And he calls her ‘a daughter of Abraham’. She belongs to God's people, with every promise made to Abraham. Later Luke will tell of Jesus calling Zacchaeus ‘a son of Abraham’ (19:9). Both had been pushed to the edge. Jesus names them as family.
passages.ot:
The Sabbath command, as Moses repeats it, is tied to freedom: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day” (Deuteronomy 5:15). A day given to remember being set free is the right day to set a woman free.

In Mark Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).
passages.hard:
Luke says the woman was disabled ‘by a spirit’ and that Satan had kept her bound. Does that mean disability or illness comes from evil spirits, or from the sufferer's sin? No. Luke does not say she had sinned, and Jesus calls her a daughter of Abraham, not a sinner. Luke also keeps sickness and possession apart elsewhere (6:18; 7:21). The Gospel does not teach that every disability or illness has an evil spirit behind it, and it would be wrong and cruel to say so of anyone today. Illness of body or mind is illness. What Luke does show is that Jesus sees suffering as something that does not belong in God's world, something he came to undo.

And if you live with a disability or a long illness that has not been healed, this story is not a judgment on your faith. The woman did not even ask. Jesus came to her. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body.
passages.asks: The synagogue leader saw a rule broken. Jesus saw a daughter of Abraham bent over for eighteen years. Ask whether your rules, even good ones, have ever stood between someone and help. And if you are the one bent low, carrying something for a long time, hear that Jesus sees you and calls you over. The Sabbath was made as a gift.

passages.t: The mustard seed and the leaven
passages.happening:
Jesus asks, “What is the kingdom of God like? To what can I compare it?” (verse 18). It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds nested in its branches.

Again he asks, “To what can I compare the kingdom of God?” (verse 20). It is like leaven that a woman mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.
passages.hearers:
Matthew has both these little parables (Matthew 13:31-33), and the note there explains them. The plant was most likely black mustard. Its seed is a millimetre or two across, and in one season the plant can grow two or three metres high. Leaven was a lump of old dough kept back from the last baking and worked into the new batch to make it rise. Three measures of flour was a large batch, the amount Sarah used to bake for her three visitors (Genesis 18:6).

Luke places the two parables right after the healing of the bent woman. A synagogue leader had just tried to stop what Jesus was doing. The kingdom looks small and easy to oppose: one woman set free in one village synagogue. But Jesus says it is like a seed that becomes a tree and leaven that works through the whole batch. Small beginnings, great endings.

In Luke a man plants the seed and a woman works the leaven. Luke often tells stories in pairs like this, one about a man and one about a woman.
passages.ot: Birds nesting in the branches of a great tree is a picture from the prophets for a kingdom that shelters the nations. Ezekiel tells of a cedar God plants on a high mountain: “Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches” (Ezekiel 17:23).
passages.hard: Leaven is often a picture of evil in the Bible. Jesus himself has just warned about “the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (12:1). So can it be a picture of the kingdom here? Yes. A picture can mean different things in different places. What leaven does, spread quietly through everything, can be bad or good. Here it is good: God's rule working its way through the whole world from the inside, unseen until everything is changed.
passages.asks: What God is doing in your life or your church may look tiny. A seed is small. Leaven is hidden. Ask whether you have dismissed something as too small to matter. Jesus says the kingdom starts that way.

passages.happening:
Jesus goes through towns and villages, teaching as he makes his way toward Jerusalem. “Lord,” someone asks him, “will only a few people be saved?” (verse 23).

Jesus answers, “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able” (verse 24). Once the master of the house gets up and shuts the door, people will stand outside knocking: ‘Lord, open the door for us.’ He will answer, ‘I do not know where you are from.’ They will say, ‘We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘Depart from me, all you evildoers.’

There will be weeping when they see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and themselves thrown out. “People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God” (verse 29). Some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.
passages.hearers:
Luke reminds us again that Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem (9:51).

Matthew has a shorter saying about a narrow gate (Matthew 7:13-14), and the note there explains it. Luke's version is a story about a house. The door is narrow, and one day it will be shut. People who knew Jesus only from a distance, who ate where he ate and heard him teach in their street, will find that this was not enough.

The great feast at the end of the age was a well-known hope: the people of God sitting at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Jesus says that people will come from every direction, from all the nations, and take their places at that table. The ones who expected to be first in line may find themselves outside.

Notice that Jesus does not answer the question he was asked. He does not say how many will be saved. He tells the questioner to make every effort to go in himself.
passages.ot: The words ‘Depart from me, all you evildoers’ echo a psalm: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping” (Psalm 6:8). The gathering from every direction echoes a psalm of thanks for people God “gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south” (Psalm 107:3). And Isaiah saw a feast for every nation: “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples” (Isaiah 25:6).
passages.hard:
Does this mean most people will be lost? Jesus refuses to give a number. Some Christians read ‘many will not be able’ as a sober statement that the saved will be fewer than the lost. Others read it as a warning to the questioner not to treat salvation as a matter of counting heads. Christians also differ on what final judgment is like, and these notes do not settle that here.

‘Make every effort’ is a strong word, the one that gives us ‘agony’. Does it mean we save ourselves by trying hard? Luke's whole Gospel says no: it is the lost who are found, and the tax collector who cries for mercy who goes home right with God (18:13-14). The effort is the effort of coming in, of not putting it off and not assuming that being near Jesus is the same as following him.

This passage is not meant to scare anyone into sleepless fear. It is an invitation: the door is there, and it is open. People will come from east and west and north and south. There is room at the table.
passages.asks: The people outside had been close to Jesus: they ate with him and heard him teach. Ask whether being near church, near Christian friends, near the things of God, has become a substitute for coming through the door yourself. And notice who is at the table: people from every direction. Who might you be surprised to sit beside?

passages.t: ‘Go tell that fox’; the lament over Jerusalem
passages.happening:
At that very hour some Pharisees come and warn Jesus: “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You” (verse 31).

Jesus answers, “Go tell that fox, ‘Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal’” (verse 32). He must keep going, “for it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem” (verse 33).

Then he cries out, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!” (verse 34). Your house is left to you desolate. “And I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord’” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Herod here is Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee and the land east of the Jordan under Rome, and who had already beheaded John the Baptist (9:9). His threat was real.

Notice who brings the warning: Pharisees. Not all Pharisees opposed Jesus, and some cared enough to warn him. The note on Matthew 23 explains who the Pharisees were. ‘Pharisee’ is not a word for a hypocrite.

A fox was known for cunning, and perhaps for doing damage. Some readers think the word also says that Herod is not to be feared. Jesus will not run from him. He has his own work to finish and his own day to finish it. ‘On the third day I will reach My goal’ speaks first of a short, set time, but Luke's readers, who knew that Jesus rose on the third day, would hear more in it.

‘It is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem’ is bitter irony. Jerusalem was the city of God, and it had a long record of rejecting the prophets God sent.

Matthew has the lament over Jerusalem at the end of Jesus' woes in the temple (Matthew 23:37-39), and the note there explains it. A hen gathering her chicks under her wings is one of the tenderest pictures in the Gospels. A hen is not a strong animal. When danger comes, she spreads her wings and puts her own body between her chicks and the threat. In Luke the words come before Jesus has reached the city. When he does reach it, “He wept over it” (19:41).
passages.ot:
The picture of God's wings is old. Boaz blessed Ruth by “the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge” (Ruth 2:12). A psalm promises, “He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4).

The warning about the house echoes Jeremiah: “this house will become a pile of rubble” (Jeremiah 22:5). The last words come from Psalm 118: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” (Psalm 118:26).
passages.hard:
What does ‘until you say, Blessed is He who comes’ mean? In Luke the words come true in part only a few chapters later, when the crowd of disciples greets Jesus on the road into the city: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” (19:38). Readers also take them further. Many hear hope in them: a day will come when Jerusalem will welcome Jesus with the words of the psalm. Others read a warning that the city will next see him when he comes as judge. Some hold both. These notes do not choose. All agree that the words are spoken with love, not hatred.

This is grief, not a verdict. The lament is not a sentence passed on the Jewish people. It was spoken by a Jew who loved Jerusalem, who longed to shelter it, and who wept over it.
passages.asks: Jesus would not be hurried by a powerful man's threat, and he would not stop loving a city that would kill him. Ask what threat has been pushing you off the work God gave you. And hear his longing: ‘how often I have longed to gather your children’. If you have been unwilling, he still longs to gather you under his wings.
